Half-space phases and the Fresnel transition

A boundary changes the powers in stationary phase. A noncritical normal direction contributes an endpoint factor of order . A critical normal direction contributes order , and odd Taylor terms can survive because only half of the integration region is present. When a real critical point crosses the boundary, a Fresnel integral describes the transition.

Write , and put The amplitude is smooth and compactly supported in a sufficiently small neighborhood of zero. The complex smooth phase satisfies on that neighborhood in the closed half-space. Smoothness there means restriction of a smooth function on an open neighborhood.

All remainders below are absolute estimates. The nontrivial stationary assertions have . If instead , a smaller support has a strictly positive imaginary lower bound and the whole integral is exponentially small. We discuss that case explicitly after the stationary formulas.

Earlier proofs and the Gaussian branch

  • Point sources and complex Gaussian kernels, Lemma 2.1 and Theorem 3.1, proves the determinant branch and the complex Gaussian integral, including semidefinite imaginary parts. Weighted cancellation for complex phases, Theorem 1, supplies the earlier cancellation estimates.
  • Regular level sets and transverse convolution, Lemmas 0.1–0.2, proves the inverse and implicit maps used to flatten a smooth boundary. Zero hypersurfaces as curvature measures, Lemma 3.0, proves nonlinear change of variables.
  • The scalar foundation, §§12–13, supplies compactness, smooth cutoffs and Taylor's integral formula. The integration foundation, §§15–16, supplies Fubini, dominated convergence and one-variable integration by parts. The finite algebra foundation, §10, supplies determinant and inverse identities.

The critical point is . Negative places it inside the half-space and positive outside. At zero the leading coefficient is half of the full Gaussian. The large positive tail agrees with the oriented normal endpoint factor, while reflection recovers the full Gaussian on the interior side.

Smooth boundaries and examples

Locally a smooth boundary is a graph , after a rigid coordinate change. Choose the sign so the domain is . The map has determinant one and a smooth explicit inverse. The earlier change-of-variables theorem therefore reduces the integral exactly to (B1). For a general flattening map the transformed amplitude includes its absolute Jacobian. One applies the preceding results to that transformed phase and amplitude; no coordinate-invariant coefficient is inferred by dropping a Jacobian.

These amplitudes are not compact, but inserting a compact cutoff equal to one near zero changes either integral by an exponentially small quantity: on its complement the positive imaginary phase has a positive minimum, and its Gaussian or exponential tails are integrable with the same bound after extracting half that minimum.
